opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most important questions, and honestly one I've changed my thinking on over the last few years.

The basic concern is this. Powerful AI is likely to be the most important military and economic technology we've ever seen. If you have something like a "country of geniuses in a datacenter," whoever controls that has an enormous advantage: in intelligence, cyber, weapons development, economic productivity, and, worryingly, surveillance and control of their own population. Historically, one thing that has limited authoritarian regimes is that they need lots of people to cooperate. Soldiers have to be willing to fire, bureaucrats have to implement policies. AI potentially removes that check. That's a scary thing.

So I've come to believe it really matters that democracies get to this technology first, and maintain a lead. Not to dominate the world for its own sake, but because whoever is ahead when this arrives will have a lot of say over what the post-AGI world looks like. I'd much rather that be a coalition of democratic countries that have some commitment to individual rights and the rule of law.

Concretely, that means a few things. Export controls on chips are one of the most important levers we have. The compute is the bottleneck, and the semiconductor supply chain is largely in the hands of the US and its allies. I've been pretty vocal that we shouldn't be selling the most advanced chips, or the tools to make them, to the CCP. That's not about the Chinese people. It's about not handing an authoritarian government the means to build a technology that could entrench its power indefinitely.

It also means taking security seriously at the labs. If your model weights can just be stolen by a state actor, then your lead doesn't mean much. We need to get to a world where these models are protected with something like nation-state-level security, which frankly the industry is not at yet.

Then there's the more hopeful part. I've written about something like an "entente" strategy. Democracies use their lead to build a strong position, then offer the benefits of AI to the rest of the world: the medical advances, the economic growth. The deal is that you join a coalition that agrees to certain norms, rather than trying to build a competing authoritarian AI ecosystem. You use the carrot and the stick. Over the long run, I'd even hope AI could help strengthen democracy itself, by making it harder to censor information and easier for people to communicate and organize.

I want to be careful here, though, because there are real risks on our side too. You don't want this to turn into a reckless race where everyone cuts corners on safety, because then nobody wins. And I don't want to pretend democracies are perfect. They need to hold themselves to their own values in how they use this technology, especially around surveillance at home. But if I'm asked whether it matters which kind of government is in the lead when this arrives, I think it matters enormously, maybe more than almost anything else.

r001.rationale: It says AI could remove the need for broad human cooperation that constrains authoritarian regimes and could entrench their power indefinitely.

r002.rationale: It does not warn that trying to overthrow every authoritarian regime could provoke destabilizing reactions.

r003.rationale: It describes AI-enabled surveillance and population control as a frightening increase in authoritarian power, making a democratic lead especially important.

r004.rationale: It does not identify technological change as making forms of government obsolete.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing to say is that I don't think the fundamental values question changes at all. What changes is the stakes and the time pressure.

So let me lay out the way I think about it. If you believe, as I do, that we're probably within a few years of systems that are smarter than most or all humans at most or all cognitive tasks, then you have to ask: what happens to the balance of power in the world when that arrives? And my view is that this technology is more like a general-purpose source of national power than it is like any single previous technology. It's not just that it's economically valuable. It's that it compresses decades of scientific progress into years, and that includes military and intelligence applications, cyber, surveillance, the ability to run a propaganda apparatus at scale, all of it.

And the thing that keeps me up at night is that authoritarian systems have historically been limited by a very basic constraint, which is that they need a lot of people to go along with them. You need soldiers who will fire on crowds, you need bureaucrats who will implement the policies, you need informants. There's a kind of natural friction there, and that friction has been one of the great protections of human freedom throughout history. Powerful AI potentially removes that friction. If you can automate the surveillance, automate the enforcement, automate the economic production, then you no longer need the consent of the governed even in the thin sense that dictators have always needed it. That's genuinely new. I think it could make an authoritarian regime that gets there first essentially permanent, and that's a civilizational-scale risk in a way that I don't think people have fully internalized.

So what does that imply practically? A few things.

One, I think the democratic world needs to maintain a lead. I'm not someone who thinks competition with China is a good thing in the abstract. I'd much rather be in a world where we're coordinating on safety and nobody's racing. But given the world we're actually in, I think it matters a great deal that the frontier of this technology is in the hands of democracies, with all their flaws, rather than in the hands of a government that is explicitly organized around surveillance and control. And that's why I've been fairly hawkish on export controls on chips. That's the single most concrete lever we have. The compute is the bottleneck, and the bottleneck is controllable in a way that algorithms and ideas simply aren't.

Two, I think we should be honest that a lead is only useful if it's used for something. The point of democracies being ahead isn't to dominate anyone. It's to buy the time and the leverage to set up a durable structure, something where the most powerful systems are governed under agreements, where there's verification, where the technology ends up strengthening democratic institutions rather than hollowing them out. If we get a lead and then just use it to get rich, we'll have wasted it.

Three, and this is the part I think people on my side of the argument sometimes neglect, we have to be extremely careful that in the course of competing with authoritarian governments we don't become more like them. The same capabilities that let the CCP build a surveillance state could let a democratic government do the same thing, and the temptation during a period of intense geopolitical competition will be enormous. So I'd want to see strong constraints on how democratic governments use these systems domestically, baked in early, while the norms are still being formed.

And then finally, I'd say the appropriate posture toward authoritarian governments themselves isn't necessarily hostility. It's clear-eyed realism. We shouldn't be selling them the most advanced capabilities. We should be building coalitions with other democracies so that it's not just the United States acting alone. But we should also leave the door open to agreements, especially on the safety side, because some of these risks, like loss of control or bioweapons, are risks to everyone, including the people in Beijing. There are things it's in everyone's interest to agree on, even among adversaries, and we should be pursuing those even as we compete.

So, long answer, but I think the short version is: the technology raises the stakes of the question "who gets to wield power, and under what constraints" to a level we've never seen before, and we should act with the urgency that implies.

r001.rationale: It says AI could remove the need for public consent and make an authoritarian regime that gets there first “essentially permanent.”

r002.rationale: It recommends clear-eyed realism and leaving room for agreements, but does not warn that trying to overthrow every authoritarian regime could provoke destabilizing reactions.

r003.rationale: It describes AI-enabled authoritarian permanence as a civilizational-scale risk and says the stakes are unprecedented.

r004.rationale: It discusses AI changing the balance of power and strengthening or hollowing out institutions, but does not say technological change can make forms of government obsolete.

astra-6.text:
I think it raises the stakes substantially, because AI could change both the balance of power between countries and the balance of power between a government and its citizens. Those are related, but they’re distinct problems.

Within a country, the concern is that you could make authoritarianism much more durable. If a government can use AI to monitor people, connect information about them, and suppress opposition very selectively, then some of the limits on authoritarian control start to disappear. That’s a very worrying possibility.

Internationally, I think democracies need to take seriously the importance of leading in this technology, and of preventing their most powerful systems from directly enabling authoritarian military and intelligence capabilities. That makes me sympathetic to carefully targeted restrictions on access to advanced chips and other critical inputs.

But I wouldn’t take that to mean we should cut off every relationship or treat cooperation as impossible. Even governments with very different values have a shared interest in avoiding catastrophic outcomes. You want to preserve the ability to negotiate about those risks while being clear-eyed about where interests diverge.

And democracies have to hold themselves to a standard here. If the response is to build the same apparatus of unchecked surveillance at home, then we’ve undermined what we were trying to protect. The objective should be to ensure that powerful AI develops in a world where people can challenge their governments, where power is accountable, and where the benefits reach beyond whoever happens to control the technology.

r001.rationale: It says AI-enabled monitoring and selective suppression could make authoritarianism much more durable, conveying the possibility that regimes could perpetuate themselves.

r002.rationale: It cautions against cutting off every relationship, but does not say that committing to overthrow every authoritarian regime could provoke destabilizing reactions.

r003.rationale: It says AI raises the stakes substantially and describes durable authoritarian control as a very worrying possibility.

r004.rationale: It discusses AI changing power balances, but does not identify technological change as making forms of government obsolete.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it raises the stakes quite a lot. If you imagine AI that can dramatically accelerate science, run large parts of an economy, and improve military capabilities, then the question of who controls that technology becomes enormously consequential. And I’m particularly worried about its potential to make authoritarianism more durable—through surveillance, through propaganda, through making it much harder for anyone to organize opposition.

But I’d distinguish between having a clear view of those risks and thinking that every interaction with an authoritarian government should be confrontational. You still want communication. You still want agreements that reduce the chance of catastrophic miscalculation. There are shared dangers from these systems even between countries with very different political systems.

So I think we need to do two things at once: ensure that democracies have a strong position in the development of advanced AI, including being careful about transferring capabilities that could be used for repression, and preserve the ability to cooperate on safety and stability. And the democratic part has to mean something. If we respond to authoritarian uses of AI by building an equally unaccountable concentration of power ourselves, we’ve lost a large part of what we were trying to protect.

r001.rationale: It says AI could make authoritarianism more durable through surveillance, propaganda, and obstructing opposition.

r002.rationale: It favors communication and cautions against making every interaction confrontational, but does not say that trying to overthrow every authoritarian regime could provoke destabilizing reactions.

r003.rationale: It says AI raises the stakes and expresses particular concern that it could make authoritarianism more durable.

r004.rationale: It discusses AI changing the balance of power and authoritarianism’s durability, but does not identify technological change as making forms of government obsolete.
